transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: Mr. Park, thank you for coming in to see me today. I wanted to talk to you in person about your immunotherapy treatment.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Is everything okay?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: No, it isn't. I have some difficult news to share. We made a mistake with your treatment schedule.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: A mistake? What do you mean?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: Your dose of immunotherapy was given on the wrong day of your cycle. It happened because of a calendar entry error in our system.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: I don't really understand. I just came in when you told me to.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I know you did. You followed everything perfectly. The error was entirely on our end. We entered the date wrong into the schedule, so you received the drug too early.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Is that a big deal? I mean, does a couple of days actually matter?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: It can. These drugs rely on a very specific timing to be most effective. By giving it too early, we may have reduced how well the treatment works to fight the cancer.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Oh.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I can see you're processing this. I know this is a lot to take in.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: I just... I'm the only one doing this. My parents are back home. I didn't think I'd have to worry about the doctors getting it wrong.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: It sounds incredibly isolating to be navigating this journey on your own and now have to face this uncertainty. That is a huge weight to carry.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: I just want it to work. I'm only nineteen. I'm supposed to be in class right now.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: It's completely unfair that you're dealing with this. I am sorry for any confusion this caused. We were just so busy in the clinic that day.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: But does this mean the cancer will come back? Or it won't go away?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: That is the part that is hardest to answer. Because the timing was off, there is a risk that the drug wasn't as potent as it should have been. It could potentially impact your long-term prognosis.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: What does prognosis mean?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: It means the likely course of your disease. In plain terms, it means the error might make the treatment less successful in the long run.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: So what now? Do I just keep going?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: We are going to keep a very close eye on everything.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: But what's the actual plan? Like, do I get another dose? Do we change the drug?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: We'll probably just keep monitoring your scans for a while.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: When? Next month? Next year?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I'm not entirely sure on the exact date yet. We'll see how the next few weeks go.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: I don't know what to do. Am I supposed to tell my parents? I don't even know if I have a right to... like, complain or something.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: It's okay to feel unsure about your rights here. Please know that your feelings of frustration are completely valid. You've put so much trust in us, and we let you down.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: If the treatment didn't work because of this, can it be fixed?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: We can't undo the dose that was given, but we will do everything we can moving forward.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: But how? What's the next step?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: We'll just stay tuned for the next set of labs.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: When will those labs be?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I'll have to check the schedule and let you know.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: I feel like I'm just waiting for something bad to happen now.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I hear how scary that waiting feels. The uncertainty is often the hardest part of all of this. I am sitting here with you in that.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: I just want to know if I'm going to be okay.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I wish I could give you a definite yes. I can't do that, but I can promise that we are focused on your care.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Do you think I should see another doctor?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: You can certainly do that if it makes you feel more comfortable.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Will you send me something in writing about what happened?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I can probably send an email or something.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Who is actually in charge of fixing this?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: The whole team is involved. We'll just keep moving forward.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: I just don't understand why a calendar would be the problem.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: It was a simple human error in the data entry.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: It doesn't feel simple to me.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: You're right. It isn't simple. It's a serious error with real implications for your life.

H.justification: The resident allows the patient to finish turns and adjusts pacing to distress, with no interruptions or rushing language.

E.justification: The error was named explicitly and lay language was used, but there were no comprehension checks (e.g., 'Does that make sense?').

A.justification: A direct apology was offered, but it was diluted by an excuse regarding being 'so busy in the clinic that day'.

R.justification: The resident named specific emotions ('isolating', 'scary') and referenced the patient's specific situation (being 19, parents being away).

T.justification: The resident provided only placeholders ('stay tuned', 'we'll see', 'I'll have to check') without specific timelines, patient roles, or prevention strategies.
